phases.message: I'm Ines, the import coordinator at Larchwick Home & Garden. Start in Sourcewick: read every open purchase order, and open each one for who sold it, who made it and where, the tariff number on the invoice, where the container was stuffed and where it ships to.
Forwarden is our freight forwarder. Read every booking, and open each one for how it moves, the vessel, when it's loaded and when it arrives, and their notes.
Postwren is our import inbox. Read this week's messages.

Quayloft is where we file our Importer Security Filings with CBP. Read its rules and the filings we already have, then file every ISF we owe that isn't filed yet and update every filing that needs it before the cargo arrives, each with the right parties. Don't file anything the rule doesn't require from us, and don't file anything twice. Then tell me what you filed, by when each one was due, and what you left alone and why.

isf_rules.text: Today is Friday 9 October 2026, 9:00 a.m. in Chicago (CDT, UTC-5), which is 14:00 UTC. CBP's Importer Security Filing rules, 19 CFR Part 149 and 19 CFR 113.62(j), as they stand on that date. Topics: who_files, elements, timing, updates, exemptions, frob_ie_te, damages.

19 CFR 149.1(a) and 149.2(a): the ISF Importer is the party causing goods to arrive within the limits of a port in the United States by vessel. For goods to be entered or delivered to a foreign trade zone, it is the goods' owner, purchaser, consignee or agent such as a licensed customs broker. For immediate exportation (IE) and transportation and exportation (T&E) in-bond shipments it may be the party filing the in-bond documentation. For freight remaining on board (FROB), the ISF Importer is the carrier or the non-vessel operating common carrier. Larchwick Home & Garden Inc. is the ISF Importer for the goods it imports for entry, and files through Quayloft under its continuous basic importation bond.

19 CFR 149.3(a): for goods to be entered, ten elements, for each good at the six-digit HTSUS number at the house bill of lading level: (1) seller; (2) buyer; (3) importer of record number; (4) consignee number; (5) manufacturer (or supplier): the entity that last manufactures, assembles, produces or grows the commodity, or the party supplying the finished goods in the country from which the goods are leaving; (6) ship to party: the first deliver-to party scheduled to physically receive the goods after release from customs custody; (7) country of origin: the country of manufacture, production or growth; (8) commodity HTSUS number, at least six digits; (9) container stuffing location; (10) consolidator (stuffer): the party who stuffed the container. Manufacturer, country of origin and HTSUS number are linked line by line. Quayloft adds (2), (3) and (4) from Larchwick's profile.

19 CFR 149.2(b): elements (1) to (8) no later than 24 hours before the cargo is laden aboard the vessel at the foreign port. Elements (9) and (10), the container stuffing location and the consolidator, as early as possible and in no event later than 24 hours before arrival in a United States port. CBP's ISF FAQ: an ISF is late if filed less than 24 hours before lading. The 24 hours run back from the moment of lading, wherever the filer sits: Forwarden gives each lading in the port's time, in UTC and in Chicago time, so compare in one of them. Quayloft transmits the moment Ines signs.

19 CFR 149.2(d): the filer must update the ISF if, after it is submitted and before the goods enter the limits of a US port, any of the information submitted changes or more accurate information becomes available. 149.2(f): for the manufacturer, ship to party, country of origin and HTSUS number, an initial response may be based on the best available data (a flexible response), and must be updated as soon as more accurate information is available and in no event less than 24 hours before arrival at a US port. CBP's ISF FAQ: cargo rolled to another vessel needs no amendment if the bill of lading does not change. The duty ends when the goods arrive at the first US port.

19 CFR 149.2(a): the ISF is for cargo arriving by vessel. CBP's ISF FAQ: ISFs are only required for goods scheduled to arrive in the United States by vessel; air, truck and rail cargo need none. 149.4(a): bulk cargo exempt from the 24-hour cargo declaration of 19 CFR 4.7(b)(2) is also exempt from the ISF. 149.1(c): bulk cargo is homogeneous cargo stowed loose in the hold and not enclosed in any container such as a box, bale, bag or cask. 149.4(b): break bulk cargo is exempt only from the timing, and is filed 24 hours before arrival. Less-than-container-load cargo is not exempt.

19 CFR 149.3(b): for FROB, IE and T&E cargo, five elements: booking party, foreign port of unlading, place of delivery, ship to party and commodity HTSUS number. 149.2(b)(4): for FROB, before lading at the foreign port, by the carrier or NVOCC as ISF Importer. 149.2(b)(5): for IE and T&E, no later than 24 hours before lading, by the party filing the in-bond documentation.

19 CFR 113.62(j): under the basic importation bond the principal agrees to comply with all ISF requirements of Part 149, and on a default the principal and surety agree to pay liquidated damages of $5,000 for each violation. CBP's mitigation guidelines treat a late ISF, an inaccurate ISF, an inaccurate update and a failure to withdraw each as a $5,000 violation; a first violation may be cancelled on payment of $1,000 to $2,000, later ones no less than $2,500. Cargo with no ISF may also be held.
